messages.mes:
The road took him at its own pace. Cart ruts, dry mud, a line of geese being driven by a boy with a switch—the ordinary morning of a frontier city assembling itself around him. Ashbridge grew as he walked: first the wall, gray stone patched in places with paler, newer masonry, then the gate ahead of him with a short queue of farmers and a pair of watchmen in dull mail who looked at faces and loads without much interest.

One of them glanced at the staff slung across Alaric's back, at the plain robes, and moved on to the next cart. Nobody stopped him. The gate arch smelled of straw and old smoke, and then the noise of the city closed over him—hammers somewhere, a woman calling a price, gutters running with wash-water.

He asked nothing and needed to ask little. The Guild's board stood out over a side street off the market square: a painted shield and crossed swords, flaking a little at the edges. Through the open door came the smell of ink, leather and last night's ale.

Inside was busier than the street suggested. A long notice board covered one wall, thick with overlapping slips. Two tables of adventurers sat over maps and breakfast both, a woman in scale mail argued quietly with a man in a Guild clerk's tabard, and behind the counter a younger clerk with ink-stained fingers was copying entries into a ledger, quill scratching.

She looked up when the door moved, took in the staff, the robes, the face she clearly didn't know, and said, "Morning. Counter's here if you're after business—board's free to read."

Then she went back to her ledger, because there was nothing in him yet that required more than that.

"Alaric Red." The clerk set her quill down in the ledger's groove and pulled a fresh slip of paper toward her. "Registration's a one-time fee of two silver. That covers your entry in the rolls, your Guild mark, and the contract slips themselves—everything after that's free to take."

She reached under the counter and set out a small flat stone, dull gray, worn smooth at the edges, and left it sitting between them like it was part of the routine.

"Two things to be clear about, because people mix them up." She tapped the stone without picking it up. "Guild rank and your strength aren't the same thing. Guild rank's ours—Novice, Proven, up to Legend. It's what work you're allowed to take. Your Power Rank is what you actually are, F through S. The stone reads it. We write it down, but we don't grant it, and we can't raise it. That part's yours."

The woman in scale mail at the other counter had given up arguing and stamped out, boots loud on the boards. One of the map-table adventurers looked up at the noise, then back at his breakfast.

"So," the clerk said, and turned the fresh slip around to face him. Blank lines waited for a name, an age, a place of trade if he had one. "Two silver, a few details, one hand on the stone, and you're a Novice with a board full of work outside your rank. That's the whole of it."

She waited, hand resting open near the fee tray.

messages.mes:
The two silver coins crossed the counter with a dull click, and she swept them into the fee tray before picking up the quill again.

"Name's already given. Age?"

She took his answers in short strokes, asked nothing more personal than his trade, and left that line empty when he had none to give. Then she turned the slip aside to dry and pushed the gray stone an inch closer to him.

"Hand flat on the stone. Hold it there a moment."

The stone was cool under his palm. For a breath nothing happened, and then a faint warmth stirred against his skin and a dull amber light seeped up through the gray, swirling once before it settled into a slow, steady pulse.

"F." She noted it on the slip without ceremony. "That's honest work, at your stage. Most start there."

She dipped the quill, finished the entry in the ledger—name, age, rank, the Guild's own Novice mark beside it—and then reached under the counter a second time and set a small metal plate on the wood. Palm-sized, stamped with the Guild's shield and crossed swords, a fresh number punched at the bottom edge.

"Your Guild plate. Don't lose it; replacing one costs more than joining did." She slid the plate toward him along with a thin contract slip, the paper carrying a faint, even shimmer where the light caught it. "That's a blank slip. When you take work off the board, the desk marks it active, and when it's done you bring it back here with whatever proof the job needs, and we settle it. Nobody else closes Guild work—no village headman, no client. Just a Guild counter."

She capped the inkwell and finally gave him a proper look, the measuring kind, taking in the staff and the robes again with the number F sitting fresh in her mind.

"Board's that wall. Anything marked for Novices is yours to take. Anything higher, don't bother asking." She picked her quill back up. "Questions, or are you reading?"

messages.mes:
The south gate let him out onto a rutted cart road, and Ashbridge fell behind him in a few hundred paces—thatch and smoke and the clatter of the morning market thinning to hedgerows and wet grass. Carts passed him heading in, one loaded with turnips, the carter giving the robed young man with a staff a flat, incurious look.

Half a mile out, east of the road, the smell arrived before the sight did: old charcoal, sharp and sour, layered under something rank and animal that had no business near a kiln.

The kilns sat in a long row on a shelf of trampled ground above the clay pits—beehive shapes of dark brick, maybe a dozen of them, their mouths yawning toward the road. Some had lost chunks of their domes; weeds grew hip-high between them. Charcoal dust still blackened the ground in a wide fan, staining it gray even under the grass. The clay pits below sat flooded and idle, a single rusted barrow tipped over at the pit's edge.

Nothing moved at first. Then, near the third kiln from the road, something small and quick darted from one dark mouth to another—low, scuttling, gone before the eye could fix on it. A moment later, from somewhere inside the row, came a thin yapping sound, answered by another, then a third, the calls bouncing off the brick until it was hard to tell how many voices made them.

The wind shifted, carrying the rank smell stronger, and somewhere among the kilns something heavy scraped against brick and went still.

messages.mes:
The grass between the kilns came up to his chest in places, and the charcoal dust did him one favor: the ground near the row was bare and quiet, his boots pressing soft prints into gray powder instead of snapping weeds.

He moved kiln to kiln, keeping the brick at his shoulder, staff held low and angled. The yapping had settled into an uneven rhythm—a burst, silence, then an answer from farther down the row, the way animals call to each other while one of them keeps watch.

At the corner of the second kiln he stopped and listened. Close up, the calls resolved. Two distinct voices, thin and dog-like, coming from somewhere around the fifth or sixth kiln, where the row bent away from the road. Under them, a slower sound: claws on brick, a snuffling, wet-nosed working at something. Scavenging, or eating.

He eased his head past the curve of the dome.

Three of them, as far as he could make out. Two small ones—waist-high, hunched, hide the color of wet slate, long muzzles buried in something spread across the ground between kilns five and six. A spilled sack, maybe, dark and torn open. The third was bigger, half again their size, and it was the heavy thing he had heard: it stood half in the mouth of the sixth kiln, gripping the brick edge with clawed hands, head thrown back to scrape at something dried on the dome. Its tail, thick and hairless, switched in slow strokes.

None of them looked toward the road. The wind sat steady in his face, carrying his scent away from them and theirs toward him.

They had not seen him. The gap between kilns four and five lay open ahead, wide enough to pass through, and the two small ones had their muzzles down.

It gathered, and he swung.

The staff's end cracked across its skull mid-lunge—a flat, heavy sound like a mallet on a door. The kobold's legs folded under it and it skidded past him through the charcoal dust, plowing a furrow, coming to rest on its side with one clawed hand still opened and reaching. Its jaw worked twice against nothing. Then it went limp, breath hissing out of the scorched throat one last time, and did not move again.

The yapping stopped.

Down the row, in the narrow dark between kilns five and six, the two small ones had frozen—the one nearest with its red-jawed muzzle lifted, nostrils working, eyes straining toward the gap where he stood. They could not pick him out against the brick and grass, but they knew something was there now, something that had killed their big one in two exchanges. One of them began a low, wavering whine, and the other snapped at it to shut it up.

Then they broke. Both bolted at once—not toward him but away, scrambling up and over the curved dome of the sixth kiln, claws skittering on the old brick, and dropped down the far side toward the clay pits below, their claws ticking away over the packed earth, growing fainter.

The clearing settled. Charcoal dust drifted. The big kobold lay smoking in the gray powder a few paces off, and from the torn sack between kilns five and six came a slow drip of something dark onto the ground.

messages.mes:
The chapel yard gate swung on a raw hinge, and the cracked step by the well caught his boot heel exactly as promised. Beyond the village fence the treeline began—oak and beech mostly, the ground still soft from last week's rain—and a woodcutter's track ran into it, worn pale and littered with old chips.

The forest was cooler than the road. Damp leaf smell, the knock of a woodpecker somewhere upslope, light falling in green coins through the canopy. The track held for the first hour, then frayed into deer paths and old cart ruts grassed over, and Alaric kept his bearing by the morning sun on his left shoulder. Twice he crossed fresh hoofprints pressed deep in the mud, shod, going his own direction—somebody rode this way often enough to cut a habit into the ground.

Midday he stopped at a stream and drank from cupped hands. The water ran cold and quick, and a heron lifted off the far bank when he moved, wings creaking, unhurried as an afterthought.

The afternoon stretched longer. The wood thinned into younger birch, then thickened again, and by the time the light went long and slanted his legs had that pulled, empty feeling from walking past reason. Then the trees opened onto a cleared slope, and below it lay the river with the waystation's chimney smoking on the far bank, and beyond that, hazy in the distance, the walls of Ashbridge catching the low sun.

The waystation was closer. Its door stood open, lamplight inside, and a carter's wagon was parked in the yard with a mule still in the traces.

The river ford lay a quarter mile downstream, and Ashbridge another few hours past it.

The ford was passable in the dark only because the water ran shin-deep over the stones, brown and quick around his calves and cold enough to bite. On the far bank he wrung out his hem and kept going, the waystation's lamplight shrinking behind him.

Dark came down in earnest under the trees, then loosened where the road met open farmland. The river road was wide and hard-packed, and the moon rose enough to show the ruts. His legs went from aching to numb and back to aching. Crickets, an owl, once a fox's scream somewhere off in the fields that lifted the hair on his neck and then faded. Twice farm dogs barked at his passing and gave it up.

Past midnight the road filled with other traffic—a string of carts camped at a crossroads, their drivers asleep under canvas, embers glowing in a fire pit. One man stirred and watched him pass without a word.

Then Ashbridge. The walls came up out of the dark sooner than expected, a black mass taller than anything the road had shown for hours, and the gate stood ahead, one half shut, torches burning in the iron brackets. Two guards sat under the archway, one on a stool, the other leaning against the stone with his arms crossed. Both straightened at the sound of boots.

"Late walker." The one on the stool held up a hand, palm out. "Gate's been shut since dusk. Walkers we let in—traders and carts wait for morning." He looked Alaric over, staff and road-dust, unhurried. "Copper a head for the night watch kettle. And I'll want to know your name and business, since I'm writing it in the ledger either way."

The other guard yawned and spat into the ditch.

"Or sleep outside the walls if you'd rather keep your copper," he said. "Free. Bit damper."

messages.mes:
The copper crossed from his hand to the guard's, and the man on the stool bit it out of habit, then tucked it into a belt pouch and pulled the ledger onto his knee. A stub of pencil, worn nearly flat.

"Alaric Red. Guild business." He wrote it slow, tongue at the corner of his mouth. "From where back?"

Whatever the ledger got, it satisfied him. He shoved off the stool and put his shoulder to the half-open gate leaf, and it dragged over the stones with a groan. The other guard pushed the second leaf, and the archway opened onto the street—dark, shuttered, one lit window up a lane where a woman's voice scolded somebody, low and constant.

"Guild's on the market square," the stool guard said, settling back down. "Shut at this hour, mind. Small hours gate's left ajar for the watch, but the clerk won't see you till morning." He scratched the pencil across one last line. "Taverns off the square keep late rooms, if you've still got coin. The Salt Barrel's the one that doesn't water it."

The gate's shadow swallowed Alaric, then spat him out into the street. Night sounds of the city: a cat working something over in an alley, the far creak of the wall watch's footsteps, ash-smell from a banked forge. Cobblestones under boots instead of road mud.

The market square opened ahead, a broad dark space under the stars, the Guild hall's bulk across from it with shutters over every window and no light showing. Down the nearer lane, the Salt Barrel's sign hung from its bracket, and under its door a bar of lamplight and the murmur of a few late voices leaked into the street.

depart.reply:
The river road ran north out of Ashbridge past the last cattle pens, wide enough for two carts, packed dirt and old wheel ruts gone hard in the sun. Alaric fell in with the afternoon traffic—a woodcutter's cart, two women driving geese, a tinker who nodded once and kept his eyes on his own road.

The river kept pace to his left, sliding brown-green between reed banks. Milestones with the temple's mark counted off the distance. Farmers were cutting hay in the near fields, and the smell of it rode the warm air along with the dust.

Past the third milestone the traffic thinned. A shrine stood at a bend, a foot-high stone with rain-dark carvings and a few copper coins in a dish; someone had left a bundle of fresh wildflowers there that morning.

The sun sat low over the western hills when the waystation came into view—a stone-and-timber hut in a clearing off the road, wood smoke rising from its chimney, a stable lean-to beside it with a mule already stabled. The keeper, a broad woman in a leather apron, was splitting kindling by the door and looked up at the sound of boots.

"Room's two coppers, floor by the hearth," she said, setting the axe down. "Stew's a copper more, and it's mutton again, so no complaining after." She wiped her hands on the apron and nodded at the sacking-wrapped bundle on Alaric's shoulder. "You'll be Guild courier going up to Thornwick, then. You're the second one this week—other fella came through three days back with a smaller packet. Fever's got them crowded, they say."

She waited, hand out for the coins.

thornwick.reply:
The stew was mutton, thick with barley, and the floor by the hearth was warm long after the fire burned down to coals. Alaric slept to the sound of the mule shifting in the lean-to and woke to gray light and the keeper already stirring the pot for breakfast she didn't offer him.

"Road's clear ahead as far as I know," was all she said, taking the empty bowl.

Morning mist hung over the river, burning off as he walked. The water ran higher than yesterday's banks suggested, brown and fast, and past the waystation the road bent toward the ford Aldric had warned of—shallow-looking water glinting over stones, a worn path leading down to it. The bridge stood a quarter mile on, and Alaric kept to the road and crossed on its old planks, the current pushing hard beneath.

By midday the fields gave way to scrub and low woodland, and Thornwick announced itself before it appeared: smoke, more of it than a village that size should make, hanging in a gray sheet over the trees. Then the rooftops—a mill, a cluster of cottages, a stone chapel with a bell tower, and beside it a longer building with its shutters open and beds visible in the windows.

The village was quiet in the wrong way. People moved between houses quickly. A woman drawing water from the well looked at Alaric's staff and called something into a doorway before walking off.

A herb smell hung over the chapel yard, and the door of the infirmary stood propped open with a chair. Inside, cots filled the room wall to wall. A woman in a stained apron over temple gray was moving between them with a cup and spoon, and she stopped when Alaric filled the doorway, taking in the sacking bundle before his face.

"You're from Ashbridge." She set the cup down on a table crowded with bottles. "Sister Oren. If that's what Aldric promised, put it here and tell me he sent instructions with it."
